teacher_guide.expected_answer: C — exactly one unique line passes through any two distinct points.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Recall the property stated in section 2.3: any two distinct points determine exactly one line.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student is not distinguishing between a straight line and curved paths; they have not grasped that 'line' in geometry means straight and infinite.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student treats the two directions of travel as two different lines, confusing the direction of traversal with the identity of the line.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has invented an incorrect condition; they may be confusing the concept with something requiring three or more points.

inclusivity.support: Let the student revisit section 2.3 and try drawing two different straight lines through the same two points to see what happens.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student: how many lines can pass through just one point, and why is the answer different from the two-point case?

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 2.4 p.16
exercise.description: Name the rays shown in Fig. 2.5 (T, A, N, B) and determine whether T is the starting point of each ray.

items.prompt: Ray OA starts at point O and passes through point A. Which statement about this ray is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: It can also be correctly named AO, because both endpoints are equivalent

options.label: B
options.text: It extends endlessly in both directions from O and A

options.label: C
options.text: It is the same as line segment OA, just written differently

options.label: D
options.text: It starts at O and extends endlessly through A in one direction

teacher_guide.expected_answer: C — a ray starts at its initial point (O) and extends endlessly in one direction through A.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Recall the ray definition: one fixed starting point, endless extension in one direction; the starting point must be written first.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student does not appreciate that the starting point is special — it must appear first and cannot be swapped, unlike a segment name.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student is describing a line, not a ray; they have not distinguished the one-directional nature of a ray from the two-directional nature of a line.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student conflates a ray (one endpoint, infinite) with a line segment (two endpoints, finite).

inclusivity.support: Let the student look back at the torch-beam description in section 2.4 to anchor the idea of one starting point and one direction.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask: if OA and OB are two different rays from O, can they be the same ray? When yes, and when no?

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 2.4 p.15
exercise.description: Help Rihan (how many lines through one point?) and Sheetal (how many lines through two points?) find their answers.

items.prompt: Three rays PA, PB, and PC share vertex P. A student labels one angle as ∠P. Why is this labelling incorrect?

options.label: A
options.text: An angle must always be named with four letters

options.label: B
options.text: P cannot be a vertex because it also lies on three rays

options.label: C
options.text: The vertex letter must come first, not in the middle

options.label: D
options.text: ∠P is ambiguous because several different angles share vertex P

teacher_guide.expected_answer: B — when multiple rays share a vertex, ∠P alone does not identify which pair of rays forms the angle; a three-letter name with vertex in the middle is required.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the angle-naming rule from section 2.5: vertex as middle letter, one point from each arm on either side.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student has invented an incorrect rule; angle names use three letters (one per arm plus vertex), not four.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student has the vertex-position rule backwards; the vertex letter belongs in the middle, which is actually the correct convention.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student has confused a point lying on a ray with a point not qualifying as a vertex; any common starting point of two rays is a valid vertex.

inclusivity.support: Let the student re-read the three-letter naming explanation in section 2.5 and try naming ∠APB and ∠APC from the same figure.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to explain in their own words why ∠P becomes unambiguous again when only two rays meet at P.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 2.5 p.19
exercise.description: Find angles in given pictures (bicycle, tiled pattern, ladder, bridge truss); draw the rays forming one angle and name its vertex.

items.prompt: Points A, B, and C are marked such that no three are collinear. Lines are drawn through every pair. List all the lines you can draw. Then name every angle formed at each intersection point, using the three-letter convention.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Three lines can be drawn: AB (or BA), AC (or CA), and BC (or CB). At the intersection of AB and AC, the vertex is A and one angle is ∠BAC (= ∠CAB). At the intersection of AB and BC, the vertex is B and one angle is ∠ABC (= ∠CBA). At the intersection of AC and BC, the vertex is C and one angle is ∠ACB (= ∠BCA). Each vertex has exactly one angle when only two lines meet there.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use the uniqueness-of-line-through-two-points property to count lines, then apply the three-letter vertex-in-middle naming rule for each angle.

inclusivity.support: Let the student sketch the three points and draw the lines one at a time, labelling each before moving to the next.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to predict how many lines and angles would result from four non-collinear points, and explain the pattern.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 2.5 p.20
exercise.description: Explain why ∠APB (where three rays from P are shown) cannot be labelled as ∠P.

items.prompt: A straight angle is formed when two rays share a vertex and their arms point in exactly opposite directions. What is true about a straight angle?

options.label: A
options.text: It is formed by a quarter turn

options.label: B
options.text: It is smaller than a right angle

options.label: C
options.text: Its arms are collinear, forming a straight line through the vertex

options.label: D
options.text: Its arms form a right angle with each other

teacher_guide.expected_answer: B — in a straight angle the two arms point in opposite directions and together with the vertex form a single straight line.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Recall from section 2.8 that a straight angle is produced by a half-turn, making the two arms collinear.

what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has confused a straight angle with a right angle; they may not have distinguished the half-turn (straight) from the quarter-turn (right).
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student has the comparison backwards; a straight angle (180°) is larger than a right angle (90°), not smaller.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student is describing the right angle, which results from a quarter turn, not the straight angle.

inclusivity.support: Let the student use a sheet of paper, open it flat, and point to the straight angle formed before and after folding.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to explain using the folding argument why bisecting a straight angle always gives exactly two right angles, not just approximately.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 2.8 p.29
exercise.description: Count right angles in classroom windows and identify other right angles in the classroom.

items.section_title: Types of Angles and their Measures
items.prompt: An angle measures 215°. Which type of angle is it?

options.label: A
options.text: Acute

options.label: B
options.text: Obtuse

options.label: C
options.text: Reflex

options.label: D
options.text: Straight

teacher_guide.expected_answer: C — 215° is greater than 180° and less than 360°, so it is a reflex angle.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the classification table from section 2.11: reflex angles lie in the range 180° to 360°.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student is applying the obtuse category (90°–180°) to a value that exceeds 180°, not recognising reflex as a separate class.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student associates 215° with 'straight' perhaps because it is 'beyond straight'; they have not retained the exact boundary of 180°.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student has significantly misclassified; they may be reading or recalling the degree value incorrectly.

inclusivity.support: Let the student look back at the classification table in section 2.11 and locate where 215° falls between the listed boundaries.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask: what is the non-reflex angle paired with 215° (i.e., 360° − 215° = 145°), and what type is that?

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 2.11 p.51
exercise.description: On dot grids, join A to other grid points to get (a) an acute angle, (b) an obtuse angle, (c) a reflex angle; mark the intended angles with curves.

items.section_title: Types of Angles and their Measures
items.prompt: A student draws an angle and measures it as 82°. Which classification is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Acute angle

options.label: B
options.text: Obtuse angle

options.label: C
options.text: Reflex angle

options.label: D
options.text: Right angle

teacher_guide.expected_answer: D — 82° is between 0° and 90°, so the angle is acute.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the classification rule from section 2.11: acute angles have measures strictly between 0° and 90°.

what_each_option_reveals.D: The student knows 90° is special but places 82° in the right-angle category, not recognising that right requires exactly 90°.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student may have used the visual impression of the drawn angle rather than the numerical boundary; obtuse is 90°–180°.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student has placed a small angle in the reflex category, indicating significant confusion about the classification boundaries.

inclusivity.support: Let the student re-read the classification list in section 2.11 and physically point to where 82° falls on a number line from 0° to 360°.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask: what is the smallest integer-degree reflex angle that has an acute complement, and how did you find it?

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 2.11 p.53
exercise.description: Draw angles of 140°, 82°, 195°, 70°, and 35° using a protractor.

items.prompt: Meena draws angle ∠PQR with long arms and angle ∠STU with short arms. When she places ∠STU on top of ∠PQR so the vertices and one pair of arms coincide exactly, the free arm of ∠STU extends beyond the free arm of ∠PQR. She concludes that ∠STU is larger. Her friend says this conclusion cannot be right because ∠PQR has longer arms. Who is correct? Justify your answer using the superimposition method.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Meena is correct. When the vertices and one pair of arms coincide exactly on superimposition, the angle whose free arm extends beyond the other's free arm is the larger angle. Arm length is irrelevant to the size of an angle — the size is determined entirely by the rotation from one arm to the other. Since ∠STU's free arm extends beyond ∠PQR's free arm on superimposition, ∠STU is the larger angle, regardless of which has longer drawn arms.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the superimposition comparison from section 2.6: the angle whose free arm extends further is larger; arm length plays no role in the comparison.

inclusivity.support: Invite the student to pair-share their reasoning before writing, using the superimposition result as the starting point.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask: what would change in the argument if, on superimposition, both free arms coincided exactly — what would that tell you about the two angles?

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 2.6 p.23
exercise.description: Fold a rectangular sheet to create angles; name and compare angles formed between the fold and the sides; make different angles by varied folding and identify the largest and smallest.

items.prompt: A classmate argues: 'I folded a sheet of paper to create a straight crease. Then I folded the paper again so that the straight crease landed exactly on itself. This second fold must give me a right angle.' Explain, step by step, why this argument is correct or incorrect, using the definition of a straight angle and the idea of bisection.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The argument is correct. A straight angle is formed when two arms are collinear, spanning 180° (a half turn). Folding the paper so the crease lands exactly on itself bisects the straight angle — it divides it into two equal parts. Since the two parts together make 180°, each part equals 180° ÷ 2 = 90°. An angle of exactly 90° is, by definition, a right angle. Therefore the second fold always produces a right angle, and this is not a coincidence but a consequence of bisecting a straight angle.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the bisection argument from section 2.8: a straight angle equals 180°, and bisecting it creates two equal angles of 90° each, which are right angles by definition.

inclusivity.support: Ask the student to talk through the argument step by step with a partner before writing, focusing on what 'bisecting' means.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask: if instead you folded the straight-angle crease so it did not land exactly on itself, what types of angles would the two parts be, and how would their measures relate to 180°?

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 2.8 p.31
exercise.description: Get a slanting crease on paper; fold to get a perpendicular crease. (a) How many right angles result? Justify they are exact right angles. (b) Describe the folding procedure so another person can replicate it.

items.prompt: A full turn is divided into 360 equal parts, each called one degree (1°). Using only this fact, explain why a straight angle measures exactly 180° and a right angle measures exactly 90°. Show your reasoning in two clear steps.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Step 1: A straight angle is formed by a half turn (the two arms are collinear, pointing in opposite directions). Since a full turn = 360°, a half turn = 360° ÷ 2 = 180°. Therefore a straight angle = 180°. Step 2: A right angle is formed by bisecting a straight angle (folding the straight angle exactly in half). Since a straight angle = 180°, bisecting it gives 180° ÷ 2 = 90°. Therefore a right angle = 90°.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Derive straight and right angle measures by halving the full turn and then halving the straight angle, using the degree definition from section 2.9.

inclusivity.support: Invite the student to use the circle-division table from section 2.9 p.34 as a scaffold — find the row for 2 equal parts and the row for 4 equal parts.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask: what would a right angle measure if a full turn had been divided into 400 equal parts instead of 360, and how would straight angle relate to it?

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out, section 2.9 p.34
exercise.description: A circle divided into 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10, and 12 equal parts is shown; write the degree measure of each resulting angle near the indicated sector.

items.prompt: Rani has two rotating-arm models. Model X has arms 3 cm long and opens to a certain angle. Model Y has arms 8 cm long and opens to the same angle as Model X. She cuts an angle-shaped slit in a piece of card by tracing Model X. Will Model Y pass through the slit? Give a reason for your answer.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Yes, Model Y will pass through the slit. Because the rotation (the angle size) of Model Y is equal to the rotation of Model X, the angle of the slit matches Model Y's angle exactly. The arm length (8 cm versus 3 cm) does not affect whether the model fits through — only the rotation between the arms matters. Longer arms do not widen the angle; they simply extend further along the same directions.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the slit-passing result from section 2.7: a rotating arm passes through an angle-shaped slit if and only if its rotation equals or is less than the slit's angle; arm length is irrelevant.

inclusivity.support: Offer the student a quick sketch of both models overlaid at the vertex and ask them to identify whether the arms open by the same amount.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask: if Model Z has arms 8 cm long but opens to a slightly larger angle than Model X, will it pass through the same slit? Change one number in the problem and re-solve.

exercise.book_ref: Activity 1, p.25
exercise.description: Students make 'rotating arms' using two paper straws inserted into the arms of a paper clip, create several rotating arms with different angles, arrange them from smallest to largest by superimposition, then perform the slit-passing challenge — tracing one rotating arm onto cardboard to make an angle-shaped slit and identifying which shuffled arm passes through it.

items.prompt: On a labelled protractor, ray OA reads 35° on the inner scale and ray OB reads 110° on the inner scale, both measured from the same baseline. Find the measure of ∠AOB.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the subtraction method from section 2.9: read both rays on the same scale and subtract the smaller reading from the larger.

inclusivity.support: Offer a visual by pointing the student to Figure it Out, section 2.9 p.36, where the same subtraction procedure is applied step by step.
inclusivity.challenge: Change one reading: if OA stays at 35° and OB moves to 160°, what is ∠AOB now, and how does the answer compare? Re-solve and classify the new angle.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out, section 2.9 p.36
exercise.description: Using the labelled protractor figure (rays O, P, Q, R, S, T, U), name all different angles and write their degree measures; determine which scale (inner or outer) to use and apply subtraction where needed.

items.prompt: A student makes a paper protractor by folding a circle. After the first fold (semicircle) the crease marks 180°. After the second fold the crease marks 90°. After the third fold, two new creases appear. What degree measures do these two new creases mark? Show how you calculated each.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: After the first fold: 180°. After the second fold: 90°. The third fold bisects each of the two 90° sections. The first new crease bisects the 0°–90° section: 90° ÷ 2 = 45°. The second new crease bisects the 90°–180° section: 90° + 45° = 135°. The two new creases mark 45° and 135°.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the successive-halving method from Activity 2, section 2.9 p.37: each fold bisects the existing section, so new crease = lower boundary + (section size ÷ 2).

inclusivity.support: Offer a number line from 0° to 180° marked at 0°, 90°, and 180°, and ask the student to find the midpoint of each half before computing.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask: what two new creases appear after a fourth fold, and what are their degree measures? Extend the pattern one step further.

exercise.book_ref: Activity 2, p.37
exercise.description: Students make their own protractor by successive paper folding: cut a circle, fold to semicircle (180°), fold again to quarter-circle (90°), fold again to mark 45° and 135°, fold once more to mark 22.5° and 67.5° etc., then unfold and label all creases, identifying angle bisectors and reading off the resulting degree measures.

items.prompt: In the figure for the problem, six angles (a–f) are drawn in varied orientations. Two of them, angle (b) and angle (e), are measured by a student using a protractor. Angle (b) appears to be roughly a quarter-turn open and the student reads 88°; angle (e) appears to be slightly more than a quarter-turn open and the student reads 97°. Without using a protractor, classify each as acute, right, or obtuse, and state whether each reading is consistent with the visual appearance. Give reasons.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Angle (b) reads 88°. Since 88° is between 0° and 90°, it is acute. A roughly quarter-turn appearance is consistent with a measure close to (but less than) 90°, so 88° is consistent with the visual. Angle (e) reads 97°. Since 97° is between 90° and 180°, it is obtuse. An opening slightly greater than a quarter-turn is consistent with a measure just above 90°, so 97° is consistent with the visual. Both readings are plausible.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the classification boundaries from section 2.11 (acute: 0°–90°, obtuse: 90°–180°) and cross-check each numerical reading against the visual description.

inclusivity.support: Offer a number line marked at 0°, 90°, and 180°, and ask the student to place 88° and 97° on it before classifying.
inclusivity.challenge: Change the readings: if angle (b) had read 92° and still appeared 'roughly a quarter-turn', would that reading be consistent? Explain what error in technique might produce it.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 2.9 p.41
exercise.description: Measure and write the degree measures for six angles (a–f) drawn in varied orientations.

items.prompt: A clock has 12 equally spaced hour marks around a full circle of 360°. (a) What is the angle between two adjacent hour marks? (b) What is the angle between the hour hand at 12 and the hour hand at 4 o'clock? (c) Is the angle at 4 o'clock acute, right, or obtuse?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: (a) 360° ÷ 12 = 30° per hour mark. (b) From 12 to 4 is 4 intervals, so 4 × 30° = 120°. (c) 120° is between 90° and 180°, so it is obtuse.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Divide 360° equally among 12 hour marks, multiply by the number of intervals to find the angle, then classify using the section 2.11 boundaries.

inclusivity.support: Offer a blank clock face with 12 marks and ask the student to mark the 30° gap between marks before computing the 4 o'clock angle.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask: at which o'clock positions does the hour hand form a straight angle with the 12 position, and why? Re-solve for those positions.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 2.9 p.45
exercise.description: Angles in a clock: (a) explain why the angle at 1 o'clock is 30°; (b) find angles at 2, 4, and 6 o'clock; (c) explore other clock angles.

items.prompt: A student folds a square sheet of paper using 8 steps of origami and then unfolds it. Two creases meet at a point inside the sheet and form four angles around that point. The student measures three of them as 45°, 90°, and 135°. What must the fourth angle measure? Justify your answer.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: All four angles around a point sum to a full turn = 360°. The three known angles sum to 45° + 90° + 135° = 270°. Therefore the fourth angle = 360° − 270° = 90°. The fourth angle is a right angle.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the full-turn total (360°) from section 2.9: subtract the sum of the three known angles from 360° to find the fourth.

inclusivity.support: Offer a drawn circle divided into four sectors, label three, and ask the student what fraction is left and what its degree measure is.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask: if the four angles must all be equal and sum to 360°, what would each measure? Compare this to the right angle in the original problem.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q8, section 2.9 p.43
exercise.description: Make the origami paper-craft (8 folding steps); unfold the paper fully, draw lines on the creases and measure the angles formed.

items.prompt: Using a protractor and ruler, draw an angle of 75°. Then, without measuring again, draw a second angle equal to the first by copying the steps used to draw 75°. Write each step of the drawing procedure you followed.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Step 1: Draw a base ray from a chosen vertex point. Step 2: Place the protractor with its centre on the vertex and align the 0° mark on the base ray. Step 3: Locate the 75° mark on the correct scale and make a small dot. Step 4: Remove the protractor and draw a ray from the vertex through the dot. The resulting angle is 75°. To draw an equal second angle, repeat the same four steps from a new vertex, using 75° again at step 3. Both angles will measure 75°.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the four-step drawing procedure from section 2.10: draw base ray, align centre on vertex, locate degree mark, join to form the angle.

inclusivity.support: Offer the four-step checklist from section 2.10 as a visual scaffold while the student works through each step in sequence.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask: what would happen at step 3 if you accidentally used the outer scale instead of the inner scale for 75°? What angle would you actually draw, and how would you catch the error?

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 2.10 p.50
exercise.description: Use a protractor to draw angles of 110°, 40°, 75°, 112°, and 134°.

items.prompt: In a class guessing game, Team A draws an angle of 65° with a protractor. Team B's guesser estimates it as 80°. (a) What is Team B's score for this turn (score = absolute difference in degrees)? (b) In the next turn, Team B draws 120° but the guesser estimates 105°. What is Team A's score? (c) After these two turns, which team has the lower (better) score?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: (a) |65° − 80°| = 15°. Team B's score for turn 1 is 15. (b) |120° − 105°| = 15°. Team A's score for turn 1 is 15. (c) Both teams have a score of 15 after one turn each; the scores are equal — neither team leads.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the absolute-difference scoring rule from section 2.10's game: score = |drawn angle − estimated angle| for each turn, then compare totals.

inclusivity.support: Offer a number line and ask the student to mark both values (65° and 80°) and measure the gap between them before computing the absolute difference.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask: if Team A scores 15 in turn 1 and then 8 in turn 2, and Team B scores 15 in turn 1 and 20 in turn 2, which team wins after two turns each, and by how much?

exercise.book_ref: Let's Play a Game #1, section 2.10 p.48
exercise.description: Team game: one team secretly draws an angle with a protractor; the other team visually estimates the measure; score is the absolute difference in degrees. Each team gets five turns; lowest score wins.

items.section_title: Types of Angles and their Measures
items.prompt: The Ashoka Chakra has 24 spokes equally spaced around a full circle. (a) What is the angle between two adjacent spokes? (b) What is the measure of the angle formed between the 1st and 6th spoke (counting 5 gaps)? (c) Is this angle acute, right, or obtuse?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: (a) 360° ÷ 24 = 15° per gap. (b) 5 gaps × 15° = 75°. (c) 75° is between 0° and 90°, so it is acute.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Divide the full 360° by 24 to find the per-spoke angle, multiply by the number of gaps, and classify using the section 2.11 boundaries.

inclusivity.support: Offer a circle divided into 24 equal sectors and ask the student to count 5 sectors and shade them before computing the angle.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask: how many spoke-gaps are needed to form the largest acute angle possible (less than 90°), and how many for the smallest obtuse angle? Justify both answers.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q6, section 2.9 p.42
exercise.description: Using the protractor figure with rays A, B, C from X along base E, find the degree measures of ∠BXE, ∠CXE, ∠AXB, and ∠BXC.
